lmml:facts.text: A Hard Day's Night is a 1964 musical comedy film starring the Beatles, directed by Richard Lester and written by Alun Owen.
The film was shot in black-and-white in a cinéma vérité style influenced by the French New Wave and British kitchen sink realism.
It premiered at the London Pavilion on 6 July 1964; the film and its soundtrack were widely released on 10 July.
The opening scenes of fans chasing the band, meant to be Liverpool's Lime Street Station, were filmed at London's Marylebone Station.
Marylebone also plays the station where the band arrive in London, filmed from a different angle.
The opening sequence was filmed at Marylebone on Sunday 5 April 1964; the station was closed to the public on Sundays.
On that first Sunday over a hundred fans were filmed chasing the Beatles; the extras were paid £7 10s.
A scene was also filmed in Boston Place, with the group running towards the camera while being chased by fans.
The Beatles returned on Sunday 12 April 1964, without fans, and were filmed running down the length of a platform to catch a moving train.
Wikipedia states that filming began on 2 March 1964 at Marylebone station, and that the four Beatles had joined the actors' union Equity only that morning.
Marylebone opened to passengers on 15 March 1899 as the London terminus of the Great Central Main Line; it was the last of London's main line termini to be built and is one of the smallest.
As one of the quietest London termini, Marylebone has been popular as a filming location, also used for The IPCRESS File (1965).
Marylebone is on the Bakerloo line of the Underground.

lmml:openQuestions: Dates: Wikipedia says filming began at Marylebone on 2 March 1964, while The Beatles Bible dates the opening chase to 5 and 12 April 1964. These may be two different shoots (the train departure in March, the chase in April) but no source read says so explicitly.
The sources do not say which way the Beatles run along Boston Place, nor which platform was used: the camera position and bearing are a guess to be checked against the film.

lmml:texts.text: Run! This is where the Beatles sprint away from more than a hundred fans at the start of A Hard Day's Night (1964). The film says it's Liverpool. It's actually London. Can you run the length of Boston Place faster than Ringo?

Courez ! C'est ici que les Beatles fuient plus de cent fans au début de A Hard Day's Night (1964). Le film prétend que c'est Liverpool… mais c'est Londres. Qui court le plus vite jusqu'au bout de Boston Place ?

The first minutes of A Hard Day's Night (1964) show the Beatles being chased by fans into a railway station. The story says it is Lime Street Station in Liverpool, but the scenes were filmed here, at Marylebone. Later in the film the same station, shot from a different angle, is where the band arrive in London.

The chase was filmed on Sunday 5 April 1964, when the station was closed to the public. Over a hundred fans took part as extras, paid £7 10s each. One scene was shot in Boston Place, the street beside the station, with the group running towards the camera. A week later the four came back, without the crowd, and were filmed running down a platform to catch a moving train.

Marylebone opened in 1899 and was the last of London's main line termini to be built. It is one of the smallest and quietest, which is why film crews like it: The IPCRESS File was shot here too.

Richard Lester's A Hard Day's Night, written by Alun Owen, premiered at the London Pavilion on 6 July 1964 and went on general release, with its soundtrack, on 10 July. It was shot in black-and-white in a cinéma vérité manner that drew on the French New Wave and on British kitchen sink realism, and its opening sequence is the clearest statement of that manner: the band pursued by fans into a station that the narrative presents as Liverpool Lime Street.

The station is Marylebone. Movie-Locations identifies it both as the film's 'Lime Street' and, from another angle, as the London terminus where the band arrive, so that a single building stands at both ends of the journey. The Beatles Bible dates the opening sequence to Sunday 5 April 1964, a day on which the station was closed to the public; more than a hundred fans were filmed in pursuit, the extras receiving £7 10s, and a further scene was taken in Boston Place with the group running towards the camera. On Sunday 12 April the four returned without the crowd and were filmed running the length of a platform to catch a moving train.

Wikipedia, however, states that filming of the picture began at Marylebone on 2 March 1964, the morning on which the four Beatles joined the actors' union Equity. How this first day relates to the April Sundays is not explained by the sources consulted.

The choice of station was practical. Opened to passengers on 15 March 1899 as the London terminus of the Great Central Main Line, Marylebone was the last of the capital's main line termini to be built and remains one of the smallest; its quietness has made it a recurrent film location, used the following year for The IPCRESS File.

lmml:facts.text: Charlotte Mews is the alleyway from which the four Beatles emerge as they run to the television concert at the climax of A Hard Day's Night.
The scene comes about 70 minutes into the film.
Movie-Locations captions the scene 'The Beatles arrive in the nick of time'.
The mews is opposite the old entrance of the Scala Theatre, which the band run into, and is still unchanged.
The Scala Theatre is the 'TV studio' of the film, where the band rehearse and perform the final concert.
From 23 to 30 March 1964 filming took place at the Scala Theatre, and on 31 March the concert footage was shot there, with the group miming to backing tracks.
The Scala Theatre building used in the film opened in 1905, was designed by Frank Verity and seated 1,139.
Its name comes from the Italian word for staircase: stairways led from either side of the dress circle down to the stalls.
From 1945 the Scala presented Peter Pan every year until it closed in 1969.
A block called Scala House now stands on the site of the theatre.
Charlotte Mews is a couple of minutes' walk from Goodge Street Underground station on the Northern line.
A Hard Day's Night was directed by Richard Lester and premiered in London on 6 July 1964.

lmml:openQuestions: Demolition date of the Scala: Movie-Locations and Tokyo Fox say it was demolished in 1969; Wikipedia says it closed in 1969 and that planning permission for demolition was granted in 1972.

Address of the Scala: Movie-Locations gives 21 Tottenham Street; Wikipedia says the main entrance was in Charlotte Street, with the old Tottenham Street portico as the stage door, and gives Scala House as 25 Tottenham Street. Which door the Beatles run into should be checked against the film.
Charlotte Mews has more than one opening; the photo and the camera estimate use the archway on Tottenham Street. Confirm it is the one in the film.

lmml:texts.text: Four Beatles, one narrow alley, and a TV show about to start without them! In A Hard Day's Night the band burst out of this archway and dash into the theatre across the road. Try it: who gets across first?

Quatre Beatles, une ruelle étroite et une émission de télé qui va commencer sans eux ! Dans A Hard Day's Night, le groupe surgit de ce passage et file vers le théâtre d'en face. À vous : qui traverse le premier ?

About 70 minutes into A Hard Day's Night (1964) the film reaches its climax: the television concert is about to begin. They come running out of this alleyway, Charlotte Mews, and into the theatre opposite, 'in the nick of time'.

That theatre was the Scala. In the film it is the 'TV studio' where the band rehearse and play the final concert. The crew worked there from 23 to 30 March 1964, and on 31 March the concert was filmed, with the group miming to backing tracks.

The Scala had opened in 1905, designed by Frank Verity, with 1,139 seats. Its name is the Italian word for staircase, after the stairways that led from the dress circle down to the stalls. From 1945 it staged Peter Pan every year until it closed in 1969. A block called Scala House now stands on the site.

The theatre is gone, but the mews has not changed. Goodge Street station on the Northern line is a couple of minutes' walk away.

Charlotte Mews supplies one of the last exterior images of A Hard Day's Night (dir. Richard Lester; premiered in London on 6 July 1964). At roughly the seventieth minute, according to Tokyo Fox, the four Beatles emerge from the alleyway on their way to the television concert that closes the film. Movie-Locations notes that the mews lies opposite the old entrance of the Scala Theatre, into which they run, and that it survives unchanged.

The Scala is the film's 'TV studio', the setting of both rehearsal and concert. Wikipedia's account of the shooting schedule places the unit there from 23 to 30 March 1964, with the concert footage taken on 31 March, the group miming to backing tracks. The building then in use had opened in 1905 to designs by Frank Verity and seated 1,139; its name, the Italian for staircase, referred to the stairways descending from either side of the dress circle to the stalls. From 1945 it presented Peter Pan annually until its closure in 1969. A block named Scala House now occupies the site.

The mews therefore outlives the building that gave the scene its meaning: the visitor sees the place the Beatles ran from, not the place they ran to. The sources consulted differ on when the theatre was demolished and on its street address, and these points are recorded as open questions in the data for this location.

The mews is a couple of minutes' walk from Goodge Street Underground station on the Northern line.

lmml:facts.text: Notting Hill is a 1999 romantic comedy directed by Roger Michell and written by Richard Curtis, starring Julia Roberts and Hugh Grant.
It tells of a romance between a British bookshop keeper (Grant) and a famous American actress (Roberts) who happens to walk into his shop.
The film premiered at the Odeon Leicester Square on 27 April 1999 and opened in the UK on 21 May 1999.
On release it was the highest-grossing British film of all time.
The shop used as William Thacker's travel bookshop is at 142 Portobello Road.
At the time of filming the premises were Nicholls Antique Arcade; they later became the furniture store Gong and are now a gift and souvenir shop called 'Notting Hill'.
The gift shop copies the typeface and colours of the film title and has added a sign reading 'The Travel Book Shop'.
The real Travel Bookshop that inspired the film was around the corner at 13-15 Blenheim Crescent; it closed in 2011 and has reopened as The Notting Hill Bookshop at 13 Blenheim Crescent.
Filming began on 17 April 1998 and lasted six weeks in Notting Hill; interior scenes were filmed last, at Shepperton Studios.
Director Roger Michell feared that shooting on Portobello Road would cause gridlock and attract thousands of onlookers and paparazzi.
The song heard as Will strides down Portobello Road is 'Ain't No Sunshine' by Bill Withers.
Near the end of the film Anna comes to the bookshop with a wrapped gift and asks Will to take her back.

lmml:openQuestions: Wikipedia says 'The Travel Book Store is located at 142 Portobello Road' without distinguishing the film location from the real Travel Bookshop in Blenheim Crescent; Movie-Locations is explicit that there never was a travel bookshop at no. 142.
No source read says whether the bookshop interior was shot at no. 142 or on a set (Wikipedia only says interior scenes were filmed at Shepperton Studios).
The shop at no. 142 has changed hands several times: check what is there now.

lmml:texts.text: A film star walks into a little bookshop… and falls for the bookseller! That's Notting Hill (1999), and this is the shop front. Surprise: it was never a bookshop. Look for the sign that says 'The Travel Book Shop' anyway.

Une star de cinéma entre dans une petite librairie… et tombe amoureuse du libraire ! C'est Notting Hill (1999), et voici la devanture. Surprise : ça n'a jamais été une librairie. Cherchez quand même l'enseigne « The Travel Book Shop ».

Notting Hill (1999), directed by Roger Michell and written by Richard Curtis, is the story of a British bookshop keeper, played by Hugh Grant, and a famous American actress, played by Julia Roberts, who happens to walk into his shop. This is the shop: 142 Portobello Road. Near the end of the film she comes back here with a wrapped gift and asks him to take her back.

There never was a travel bookshop at this address. When the film was made the premises were Nicholls Antique Arcade; later they became a furniture store, and today they are a gift shop called 'Notting Hill', which copies the film's typeface and has added a sign reading 'The Travel Book Shop'.

The real Travel Bookshop that inspired the film was around the corner, at 13-15 Blenheim Crescent. It closed in 2011 and has reopened as The Notting Hill Bookshop.

Filming began on 17 April 1998 and lasted six weeks in the neighbourhood. On release the film was the highest-grossing British film of all time.

Notting Hill, directed by Roger Michell from a screenplay by Richard Curtis, premiered at the Odeon Leicester Square on 27 April 1999 and opened in the United Kingdom on 21 May; on release it was the highest-grossing British film to date. Its premise is a romance between a British bookshop keeper and a famous American actress who happens to walk into his shop, and the shop is accordingly the film's first and last important location: near the end, Anna returns to it with a wrapped gift to ask Will to take her back.

The front used for William Thacker's shop is 142 Portobello Road. Movie-Locations is explicit that no travel bookshop ever traded there: at the time of filming the premises were Nicholls Antique Arcade, subsequently the furniture store Gong, and now a gift and souvenir shop named 'Notting Hill', which reproduces the typeface and colours of the film's title and has added a sign reading 'The Travel Book Shop'. The model for the fictional business was the real Travel Bookshop at 13-15 Blenheim Crescent, around the corner, which closed in 2011 and has reopened as The Notting Hill Bookshop at no. 13. The location thus presents a film set that has been turned, after the fact, into an imitation of the fiction it once served.

According to Wikipedia, filming began on 17 April 1998 and continued for six weeks in Notting Hill, the interiors being shot last at Shepperton Studios. Michell feared that working on Portobello Road would bring gridlock and thousands of onlookers and paparazzi. The song heard as Will strides down the road is Bill Withers's 'Ain't No Sunshine'.

This is the 'blue door' of Notting Hill (1999): the entrance to the flat that the bookseller William Thacker shares with Spike. In the film Anna hides here from a tabloid scandal, and the next morning the paparazzi besiege the house and photograph Will, Anna and a half-dressed Spike on the doorstep.

The door is real, the flat is not. The rundown interior was a studio set and looked nothing like what is behind the door, which is a grand house. At the time it was owned by Richard Curtis, the film's screenwriter.

The original door was auctioned for charity. The door you see today is blue again.

The corner of Westbourne Park Road and Portobello Road, a few yards away, is where William bumps into Anna at the beginning of the film. Shooting in the streets of Notting Hill began on 17 April 1998 and lasted six weeks; the film opened in the UK on 21 May 1999.

280 Westbourne Park Road is, in the words of Movie-Locations, one of the most famous British film locations ever to grace the screen. In Notting Hill (dir. Roger Michell; UK release 21 May 1999) its door is the entrance to the flat that William Thacker shares with Spike, and the threshold on which the film's public and private worlds collide: Anna takes refuge in the flat from a tabloid scandal, and the next morning paparazzi besiege the house and photograph Will, Anna and a half-dressed Spike at the front door.

The location is a composite. Movie-Locations reports that the rundown interior was a studio set bearing no resemblance to what lies behind the door; Wikipedia adds that the house was owned by the screenwriter, Richard Curtis, and that behind the entrance stands a grand house rather than the flat of the film. Only the doorway, then, belongs to the fiction.

The door itself has a history. Wikipedia records that the original blue door was auctioned for charity and that the present door is blue again; the sources consulted do not date the sale.

The door stands a few yards from the corner of Westbourne Park Road and Portobello Road, where William bumps into Anna at the beginning of the film. The six weeks of street filming in Notting Hill began on 17 April 1998.

lmml:facts.text: Leadenhall Market was used to represent the area of London near the Leaky Cauldron and Diagon Alley in Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (2001).
The film was directed by Chris Columbus; it premiered at the Odeon Leicester Square on 4 November 2001 and was released on 16 November 2001.
As Harry and Hagrid walk through the market, Harry asks 'Can you find all this in London?' and Hagrid replies 'If you know where to go.'
The door through which Harry and Hagrid enter the Leaky Cauldron belongs to what is now The Glass House, an optician in Bull's Head Passage, and has a rounded doorway.
Inside the Leaky Cauldron, a magical brick wall leads to Diagon Alley.
Time Out reports that director Chris Columbus was struggling to find a setting for the Leaky Cauldron when he came upon the shop.
In the novel the Leaky Cauldron is on Charing Cross Road.
The optician's owner told Time Out that the front door 'looked old and decrepit' because they had not renovated: 'the perfect guise for a pub for wizards'.
For the third film, The Prisoner of Azkaban, the Leaky Cauldron moved to a shop front in Borough Market.
Leadenhall Market dates from the 14th century and is one of the oldest markets in London.
The present building, with its ornate roof painted green, maroon and cream, was designed in 1881 by Sir Horace Jones, architect of Billingsgate and Smithfield Markets.
The market is a Grade II* listed building, listed in 1972.

Leadenhall Market represents, in Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (dir. Chris Columbus; premiered at the Odeon Leicester Square on 4 November 2001, released on 16 November), the area of London near the Leaky Cauldron and Diagon Alley. The location differs in kind from the café of the first series. York Rise was a neighbourhood business borrowed for a neighbourhood comedy; here the series begins again inside a large commercial interior in the West End. The restaurant is in the Adelphi building on John Adam Street, which the description of a Wikimedia Commons photograph calls a monumental Art Deco building of 1936-38 by the architects Collcutt & Hamp. The sources consulted do not agree on the history of the building, a point recorded among the open questions.

The series that this dinner opens was the one that brought the programme its widest recognition: it won Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Comedy Series, Lead Actress and Writing, and in September 2019 Fleabag became the first British show to win Best Comedy Series at the Emmys.

Because the scene is an interior one, the camera position recorded for this location is only the street outside. No source consulted describes the dinner itself in detail.
